deck_context.source_summary: PHY4605 students receive ten distinct lecturer-assigned real-world physics problem briefs. Each group interprets its scenario, chooses a defensible model scope and added physics, designs an algorithm, implements and tests a computation, interprets evidence and hands off a reproducible investigation.
deck_context.core_claim: The strongest capstone is the most physically faithful, relevant and defensible approximation to the real process, not the most complicated code.
deck_context.assessment_boundary: The capstone is provisionally 15%: Week 06 feasibility 2%, Week 07 design review 3%, Weeks 08-11 development evidence 3%, Weeks 13-14 final investigation 5%, and individual defence/handoff 2%. Week 04 and Week 12 are formative.
deck_context.brief_assignment_boundary: Ten groups receive ten distinct briefs. No starter Live Script is required, no common solution path is prescribed, and the deck must not reveal a prescribed method or final answer for any brief.
deck_context.universal_constraints: Keep visible text in English. Do not invent numerical results, equations, data, or solution paths. Do not prescribe one graph, one method, one parameter change, or one validation pair. AI can assist modelling and coding, but it is never the validator.
deck_context.brief_detail_contract: Slides 06-10 present paired brief descriptions. For each brief, show context and broad objective, possible realism dimensions as examples, likely information or data categories without implying that a specific dataset exists, and boundary questions about model scope. Do not prescribe equations, numerical methods, code structure, required graphs, parameter changes, validation pairs or a feature checklist. Students choose and justify the scope.

slides.title: Projectile Investigations: Wind, Drag and Terrain
slides.intent: Explain Briefs 01 and 02 through context, broad objective, possible realism dimensions, likely information categories, and model-boundary questions without prescribing a method.
key_points: BRIEF 01 — Projectile Delivery in Crosswind with Quadratic Drag | Context + objective: a package or test body moves through crosswind toward an intended delivery region; investigate how convincingly the delivery outcome can be represented.
Possible realism dimensions: 3D motion, relative airflow, varying crosswind, aerodynamic properties, release uncertainty, air-density variation, lift or spin.
Likely information categories: launch or release conditions, object properties, target region, wind measurements or ranges, and any reference-trial observations actually supplied.
Boundary questions: Is a steady crosswind adequate? Is 3D motion material? Can the body be treated as a point? Which aerodynamic effects are supported by evidence?

BRIEF 02 — Projectile Launch from Elevated Terrain under Wind Shear | Context + objective: an object launches from elevated or uneven terrain while wind changes with height; investigate whether it can reach an intended or acceptable landing region.
Possible realism dimensions: wind shear, terrain profile, non-level impact surface, launch variability, atmospheric variation and local obstructions.
Likely information categories: site elevations or terrain information, wind observations at selected heights, launch conditions, object properties, and an intended landing or safety region.
Boundary questions: How much terrain is needed? Is 2D defensible? What happens outside measured wind heights? Are gusts, turbulence or obstacles material but unsupported?
Aim for defensible realism: preserve a transparent baseline; add effects that materially affect the objective and can be supported or tested; justify important omissions.

layout.composition: two equal vertical brief cards; one brief per column; each card has title, context/objective, possible realism dimensions, likely information categories, and boundary questions; ochre footer strip across the bottom

visual_elements.main_visual: subtle labelled projectile trajectory and terrain/wind-shear icons integrated into the two cards; diagrams support the text without prescribing a solution
visual_elements.supporting_elements: clearly labelled sections inside each card: Context + objective, Possible realism dimensions, Likely information, Boundary questions; bottom footer strip with the defensible-realism rule

constraints: Keep all five labels visible and readable for both briefs.

Do not prescribe equations, numerical methods, code structure, required graphs, parameter changes or validation pairs.
No equations, code, numeric results, company claims or invented data.

slides.title: Circuit Investigations: Non-Ideal Charging and Loading
slides.intent: Explain Briefs 03 and 04 through context, broad objective, possible realism dimensions, likely information categories, and model-boundary questions without prescribing a method.
key_points: BRIEF 03 — RC Charging with Leakage and Temperature-Dependent Components | Context + objective: a capacitor circuit operates where leakage and temperature may alter charging; investigate whether its intended timing, storage or threshold function remains credible.
Possible realism dimensions: leakage pathways, temperature-dependent component behaviour, tolerance, supply variation, measurement loading, ageing or self-heating.

Likely information categories: nominal component specifications, tolerance or temperature ranges, supply information, temperature records, observed charging data if supplied, and the usable operating range.
Boundary questions: Is temperature imposed or coupled to circuit heating? Which variations matter? Are parasitics supported? Over what range are the stated properties credible?

BRIEF 04 — RC Sensor Circuit with Internal Source Resistance and Time-Varying Load | Context + objective: a sensor is supplied by a non-ideal source while its connected load changes; investigate whether the signal remains usable and physically credible.
Possible realism dimensions: internal source resistance, changing load demand, sensor output behaviour, wiring and measurement loading, switching transients and sensor noise.
Likely information categories: source, sensor and load specifications; a load schedule or trace if supplied; calibration readings, sampling information, and an acceptable signal range.
Boundary questions: Are load changes abrupt or gradual? Does source regulation matter? Which parasitics are material? Is noise central or secondary to the objective?
Aim for defensible realism: preserve a transparent baseline; add effects that materially affect the objective and can be supported or tested; justify important omissions.

slides.title: Radiation Investigations: Detector Effects and Mixed Sources
slides.intent: Explain Briefs 05 and 06 through context, broad objective, possible realism dimensions, likely information categories, and model-boundary questions without prescribing a method.
key_points: BRIEF 05 — Radioactive Decay with Background Radiation and Detector Dead Time | Context + objective: a detector records a decaying source plus unrelated background events while closely spaced events may be missed; investigate how reliably source behaviour can be inferred.
Possible realism dimensions: background variation, detector dead time, efficiency, finite counting intervals, source-detector geometry, shielding and random counting variation.

Likely information categories: time-stamped or interval counts, background-only observations, detector specifications or calibration information if supplied, source references and measurement geometry.
Boundary questions: Is background stable? Is the dead-time description adequate? Can efficiency and geometry be treated as constant? Are observations near a detector-response limit?

BRIEF 06 — Two-Isotope Decay Mixture with Efficiency and Counting Noise | Context + objective: measurements contain two radioactive components with different timescales; investigate what can defensibly be learned about their combined behaviour or composition.
Possible realism dimensions: different decay timescales, isotope-dependent efficiency, background counts, finite intervals, repeated observations and counting variability.

Likely information categories: count records, measurement times, candidate isotope information, efficiency or calibration evidence if supplied, background observations and repeated measurements if available.
Boundary questions: Are isotope identities known? Can the detector distinguish signals? Is efficiency stable? Is dead time material? How much uncertainty can the data support?
Aim for defensible realism: preserve a transparent baseline; add effects that materially affect the objective and can be supported or tested; justify important omissions.

slides.title: Thermal Investigations: Changing Surroundings and Internal Heating
slides.intent: Explain Briefs 07 and 08 through context, broad objective, possible realism dimensions, likely information categories, and model-boundary questions without prescribing a method.
key_points: BRIEF 07 — Cooling with Thermal Radiation and a Changing Ambient Temperature | Context + objective: a hot object cools in changing surroundings where radiation may matter; investigate its thermal history relative to a useful, safe or observable temperature range.
Possible realism dimensions: changing ambient conditions, convection, radiation, surface properties, geometry, environmental exposure and sensor response.

Likely information categories: initial and observed temperatures, ambient-temperature records, object dimensions, mass and material information, surface-property estimates, and any reference cooling run supplied.

Boundary questions: Is a uniform object temperature defensible? Do radiative surroundings match measured air temperature? Which heat-loss pathways matter? Are gradients, moisture or phase changes supportable?

BRIEF 08 — Cooling of a Heated Object with Internal Heat Generation | Context + objective: an object continues producing heat while losing energy; investigate whether its operating temperature remains acceptable and how behaviour changes during operation.
Possible realism dimensions: time-dependent or temperature-dependent heating, convection, radiation, conduction through supports, insulation, ambient variation and control action.
Likely information categories: power or operating records, measured temperatures, ambient conditions, geometry and thermal properties, operating limits and reference observations if supplied.
Boundary questions: Is heating spatially uniform? Can one temperature represent the object? Does temperature affect generation? Which support or enclosure pathways matter? Is control relevant?
Aim for defensible realism: preserve a transparent baseline; add effects that materially affect the objective and can be supported or tested; justify important omissions.

slides.title: Force Investigations: Direction, Drag, Mass and Measurement
slides.intent: Explain Briefs 09 and 10 through context, broad objective, possible realism dimensions, likely information categories, and model-boundary questions without prescribing a method.
key_points: BRIEF 09 — Impulse on a Moving Body with Drag and Changing Force Direction | Context + objective: a moving body experiences a finite-duration force whose direction changes while resistance acts; investigate how the intervention alters subsequent motion.
Possible realism dimensions: force magnitude and direction history, drag, initial motion, dimensionality, body orientation, rotation and force-measurement uncertainty.
Likely information categories: force and direction records or ranges, event duration, body properties, initial motion, environmental information and any motion-tracking observations supplied.
Boundary questions: Is translation sufficient? Does the force act through the centre of mass? Is mass constant? Is this a short impulse or sustained actuation? Is the drag representation credible?

BRIEF 10 — Time-Varying Directional Actuator Force with Mass Change and Sensor Uncertainty | Context + objective: an actuator changes force direction while system mass changes and sensors are imperfect; investigate how confidently motion or actuator performance can be predicted.
Possible realism dimensions: commanded versus realised force, physical mass-change process, sensor bias/noise/delay, actuator limits, misalignment and external resistance.

Likely information categories: actuator commands or force records, orientation information, mass or payload history, sensor specifications and calibration evidence if supplied, initial state and reference tracking data.
Boundary questions: What enters or leaves as mass changes? Does transfer carry momentum? Are rotational effects material? Which sensor imperfections affect the objective? Is 2D defensible?
Aim for defensible realism: preserve a transparent baseline; add effects that materially affect the objective and can be supported or tested; justify important omissions.
